# The provenance file on Ekkeko

*Provenance record 142 · Ekkeko · one temple, fully accounted for.*

## Provenance

**1. The attestation.** **—**, from the tradition's own record.

**2. The narrative record.** **Ekeko and Coya in the Famine** — The best-known story of Ekeko is surprisingly recent: it was printed in 1904 by the Bolivian writer Antonio Díaz Villamil in his Exaltación de la Alasita.  In the time of drought, when the storehouses stood empty, the little man Ekeko fed his beloved Coya from his own flesh, cutting pieces from his body so that she would not starve. **The Little God Cobo Saw** — Bernabé Cobo, writing his Historia del Nuevo Mundo in 1653, is the earliest secure witness.  Among the household devotions of the Andean people he describes a small idol called Equeco, revered as a god of wealth and contentment: his image was a little figure loaded with packs and bundles, set up in the house and offered food, so that he would keep the family supplied with the small goods of life — food, clothing, coin.

**3. The current holding.** The temple at [/ekkeko/](/ekkeko/), a temple of the restored name. aSCII-equivalent form

**4. The documented resonances.** **Defense, Military & Security**, **Gaming, Fantasy & Entertainment IP**, **History, Archives & Records** — seats argued and weighted in the [pattern atlas](/patterns/), read through the myths in this temple's [Resonance File](/ekkeko/blog/resonance/).

**5. The continuing record.** Ekeko is today a national emblem of Bolivia, printed on lottery tickets, staged in civic pageants, and set on altars in houses that no longer remember the famine legend.  The Alasitas fair has travelled with Bolivian migration — to Buenos Aires, Santiago, and the Peruvian highlands, where Puno keeps its own January fair — so the little god now presides over diaspora longing as much as over household luck.

## The Emblems

The name does not travel alone. **The loaded pack** — The bundle of goods on his back — every modest desire of the household, abundance compressed into one bowed, patient burden.; **Clay figurine** — Pre-Columbian Tiwanaku figures of burden-carriers are the archaeological ancestors of the modern Ekeko images.; **Miniatures (alasitas)** — The tiny objects of the fair — money, houses, cars, diplomas — wishes bought small so the god can grow them large.. Each emblem is filed in the temple's record with its own provenance, the same discipline the spelling gets.

## For the Voice

Say "ekkeko" — two open syllables with a light glottal catch between the double k in the Aymara-influenced pronunciation; stress falls on the penult. The reconstructed line runs `/ekkeko/` — the temple's pronunciation atlas carries the phonemes one by one.
